title: A Platform-aware Compilation Framework for Fault-tolerant Quantum Computation
authors: Srushti Patil, Susan X. Chen, Andreas Juul Bay-Smidt, Stefan Alaric Schäffer, Peter Krogstrup, Stefano Paesani, Gemma C. Solomon
abstract: The compilation of an algorithm can vary significantly with the choice of physical hardware platform and error correction model. Yet, current compilation frameworks typically commit to a single architecture-hardware configuration, making it difficult to assess resource estimates across platforms. We present a platform-aware compilation framework that re-compiles a quantum circuit into a hardware-compatible instruction set as well as fault-tolerant operations and provides end-to-end resource estimates in terms of physical-qubit count, time-to-solution, and classical processing time. We benchmark the framework by obtaining end-to-end resource estimates for different compilers, each tailored to the functionalities of specific hardware modalities: connectivity, clock speed, and noise model. As part of this framework, we introduce a transversal active volume (t-AV) compilation architecture designed for the efficient execution of fault-tolerant operations in platforms supporting long-range logical connectivity. We benchmark the framework for Hamiltonian simulation of the 2D Fermi Hubbard model as well as for eigenenergy estimation of a small molecule (trimethylenemethane) as a candidate for early fault-tolerant demonstration of quantum chemistry. For the latter, we show that end-to-end quantum simulations can be achieved with $\sim10^4$ physical qubits and runtimes ranging from $10^2$ ms (photonics, superconducting) to $10^5$ ms (neutral atoms).
summary: This paper introduces a novel, platform-aware compilation framework designed to overcome the limitation of existing quantum compilers that are locked to a single hardware architecture. By re-compiling circuits for various connectivity types, it provides comprehensive, end-to-end resource estimates for quantum simulations. This is vital for guiding the development roadmap across diverse quantum hardware modalities.
main_problem: Current quantum compilation frameworks fail to account for the variability in physical hardware platforms and error correction models, hindering cross-platform resource assessment.
main_result: The authors present a platform-aware compilation framework that provides end-to-end resource estimates (qubits, time) for quantum simulations on diverse hardware modalities.
method: The framework re-compiles quantum circuits into hardware-compatible instruction sets by bridging Algorithm, Quantum Error Correction (QEC), and Hardware stacks based on connectivity.
model_or_system: The framework is benchmarked using Hamiltonian simulation of the 2D Fermi Hubbard model and eigenenergy estimation for trimethylenemethane (TMM). It analyzes three connectivity classes: nearest-neighbor, log N, and effectively all-to-all.
key_observables: Physical-qubit count, time-to-solution, classical processing time, and required code distance (d).
important_parameters: Connectivity type (local, log N, all-to-all), error rate (e.g., $10^{-3}$), and target logical error ($\le 0.01$).
main_assumptions: The analysis simplifies by focusing on rotated surface codes and assumes certain scaling behaviors for transversal gates and distillation processes.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the full FTQC pipeline, circuit compilation for different connectivity classes, and runtime scaling comparisons for TMM and Fermi-Hubbard across various architectures.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the platform-aware framework, details the compilation strategies for different connectivity classes (PPR, t-AV), and benchmarks the framework on two key quantum simulation problems (TMM and Fermi-Hubbard).
why_interesting: It provides a crucial, unified theoretical tool for comparing the resource costs of quantum algorithms across fundamentally different physical hardware architectures (superconducting, photonic, neutral atoms).
analysis_basis: full PDF text, analyzed in chunks

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Overview of the platform-aware compilation framework. (a) The full FTQC pipeline is divided into an Algorithm, a QEC, and a Hardware stack. The algorithm is expressed as a logical circuit in a universal gate set (here, Clifford+T), which the QEC code must support (surface code in this case). The hardware-informed compiler then bridges the QEC and Hardware stacks, selecting a compilation strategy from the logical operations available in the code and the platform’s connectivity, speed, and noise.
